module_title: Planning and Implementing Your Irrigation Project

lessons.title: Conducting a Farm Water Audit
lessons.body:
A water audit tells you exactly how much water your farm needs and where it will come from. Start by measuring your water sources. For a borehole, use a 20-litre bucket and a stopwatch: time how long it takes to fill the bucket. If it fills in 10 seconds, that's 2 litres per second, or 120 litres per minute. For a river or stream, measure the width, depth, and speed of the water. Multiply width (m) Ã depth (m) Ã speed (m/s) Ã 1000 to get litres per second. For rainwater, calculate your roof or catchment area in square metres and multiply by average annual rainfall in mm. For example, a 100 mÂ² roof with 800 mm annual rainfall gives 80,000 litres per year.

Next, calculate your crop water needs. Most vegetables need 4-6 mm of water per day. One mm of water over one hectare equals 10,000 litres. So for a 0.5 hectare plot of tomatoes needing 5 mm/day, you need 0.5 Ã 5 Ã 10,000 = 25,000 litres per day. If you irrigate every other day, double that to 50,000 litres per irrigation. Write this number down.

Now compare supply and demand. If your borehole gives 120 litres per minute and you run it for 4 hours (240 minutes), you get 28,800 litres per day. That is enough for 0.5 hectare of tomatoes if you irrigate daily, but not if you skip days. Adjust your crop area or irrigation schedule accordingly.

Finally, check water quality. Take a sample to a local agricultural office or use a simple test kit for salinity (EC) and pH. Most crops grow best at pH 6.0-7.0 and EC below 2.0 dS/m. If your water is salty, you may need to leach the soil with extra water or choose salt-tolerant crops like beetroot or spinach. Record all numbers in a notebook â this is your baseline for designing your system.

lessons.title: Designing a Custom Irrigation Plan
lessons.body:
Your irrigation plan must match your water audit, your field shape, and your budget. First, choose the method: drip, sprinkler, or furrow. Drip is best for vegetables and fruit trees, saving 30-50% water compared to furrow. Sprinklers suit leafy greens and cereals. Furrow is cheapest but uses more water and labour.

For drip, calculate the number of emitters. If you have 0.5 hectare (5,000 mÂ²) and use drip lines spaced 0.5 m apart with emitters every 0.3 m, you get about 33,333 emitters. Each emitter gives 2 litres per hour. To deliver 25,000 litres per day, you need 25,000 Ã· 2 = 12,500 emitter-hours. Divide by 33,333 emitters = 0.375 hours, or 22.5 minutes. That's too short; you'd rather run longer at lower flow. Use 1 litre per hour emitters: 25,000 Ã· 1 = 25,000 emitter-hours Ã· 33,333 = 0.75 hours = 45 minutes. Still short. Better to irrigate every 2 days: 50,000 litres Ã· 1 = 50,000 emitter-hours Ã· 33,333 = 1.5 hours. So run the system for 1.5 hours every 2 days.

For sprinklers, calculate precipitation rate. A common impact sprinkler covers a 12 m diameter circle (113 mÂ²) and delivers 0.5 litres per second. That is 30 litres per minute. Over 113 mÂ², that's 30 Ã· 113 = 0.265 mm per minute. To apply 5 mm, you need 5 Ã· 0.265 = 19 minutes. But you need to cover 5,000 mÂ², so you need 5,000 Ã· 113 = 44 sprinklers, which is expensive. Instead, use a smaller number and move them. For example, 4 sprinklers covering 452 mÂ², run for 19 minutes, then move to next section. You would need 11 moves to cover 0.5 ha, taking about 3.5 hours.

Design your layout on paper. Draw your field to scale, mark water source, pump, mainline, and sub-mains. Use 32 mm or 50 mm PVC pipes for mains, and 16 mm or 20 mm for drip lines. Include filters (sand filter and screen filter) to prevent clogging. Add a valve at each section so you can irrigate one part at a time. If your water source is lower than your field, you need a pump. Calculate pump size: for 25,000 litres per day over 4 hours, flow = 6,250 litres/hour = 104 litres/minute. If total head (lift + friction) is 15 m, pump power (kW) = flow (mÂ³/s) Ã head (m) Ã 9.81 Ã· efficiency. Flow = 104 Ã· 60000 = 0.00173 mÂ³/s. Power = 0.00173 Ã 15 Ã 9.81 Ã· 0.6 = 0.42 kW, so a 0.5 kW pump works. Write all this down â it's your blueprint.

lessons.title: Cost Estimation and Funding Options
lessons.body:
Before you buy anything, estimate costs. For a 0.5 hectare drip system, you need: drip lines (16 mm, 0.3 m emitter spacing) â about 1,000 m per 0.1 ha, so 5,000 m for 0.5 ha. At $0.20 per metre, that's $1,000. Mainline PVC (50 mm) â 100 m at $2 per metre = $200. Filter unit â $150. Valves and fittings â $100. Pump (0.5 kW solar or electric) â $300. Tank (5,000 litres) â $400. Labour for installation â $200. Total: about $2,350. For sprinkler system, you might spend $1,500. For furrow, $300. Always get three quotes from local suppliers.

Funding options: 1) Personal savings or family contributions. 2) SACCOs (Savings and Credit Cooperative Organizations) â many offer agricultural loans at 10-15% annual interest. 3) Microfinance institutions â loans from $100 to $5,000, but interest can be 20-30%. 4) Government subsidies â check with your local agriculture office for programs like the Kenya National Irrigation Authority or Tanzania's RIPAR. 5) NGOs â organizations like Practical Action or World Vision sometimes provide grants or cost-share. 6) Crowdfunding â platforms like Kiva or M-Changa can help if you have a clear plan.

Reduce costs by phasing: start with a small area (0.1 ha) and expand. Buy used equipment from other farmers. Use gravity instead of a pump if your water source is uphill. Make your own compost to improve soil water retention, reducing irrigation needs. Barter labour with neighbours. Keep records of all expenses â this helps when applying for loans. Remember, a well-designed system pays back in 1-2 seasons through higher yields and lower water bills.

lessons.title: Phased Implementation for Small Budgets
lessons.body:
You don't need $2,000 upfront. Start small and grow. Phase 1: Focus on the most profitable crop on a small plot, like 0.1 hectare (20 m Ã 50 m) of tomatoes. Buy a 1,000-litre tank ($80), a small solar pump ($150), and 500 m of drip line ($100). Total: $330. Install it yourself with a friend. This system can irrigate 0.1 ha if you run it 2 hours per day. Use it for one season and save the profits.

Phase 2: Expand to 0.25 ha. Add another 1,000 m of drip line ($200), a larger tank (2,000 litres, $150), and more fittings ($50). Total additional: $400. Now you can irrigate 0.25 ha. By now you have learned how to manage the system, fix clogs, and schedule irrigation.

Phase 3: Reach 0.5 ha. Add 2,000 m of drip line ($400), a 5,000-litre tank ($400), and a better filter ($100). Total additional: $900. You may need a bigger pump ($200). Over three seasons, you have spent $1,830, but you have been earning from each phase. This spreads the cost and reduces risk.

Key tips: Always buy the best quality drip tape you can afford â cheap tape clogs and breaks. Use a filter from day one. Keep a spare set of fittings. Learn to repair leaks with a punch and goof plugs. If you have a borehole, test its yield before expanding. If water is limited, use mulch (dry grass or plastic) to reduce evaporation by 30%. Plant windbreaks to reduce water loss. Join a farmer group to share tools and knowledge. With each phase, reinvest at least 30% of your profits into the next expansion. This way, your irrigation system grows with your farm and your skills.

lessons.title: Working with Local Suppliers and Experts
lessons.body:
Finding the right suppliers and experts can make or break your project. Start with your local agricultural extension officer. They are usually free and can advise on crop water needs, subsidies, and reputable suppliers. Visit your nearest office or ask your village chief for contacts. Also, talk to other farmers who have irrigation systems â they know who sells good quality pipes and who overcharges.

When buying equipment, always inspect before paying. For drip lines, check the wall thickness â thinner walls (0.2 mm) are cheaper but last only one season; thicker (0.4 mm) last 3-5 seasons. Ask for a sample and test it by bending â it should not crack. For pumps, check the flow rate and head on the label. A pump rated 10,000 litres per hour at 10 m head is different from one at 20 m head. Bring your water audit numbers and ask the supplier to match them. Get a written receipt with a warranty â at least 6 months for pumps.

For installation, you can hire a local technician. Expect to pay $50-$100 per day. Ask for references and visit a previous installation. If you want to learn, ask the technician to explain each step as they work. Many suppliers offer free installation if you buy a full kit. For maintenance, learn to clean filters weekly, flush drip lines monthly, and check for leaks. YouTube videos can help, but nothing beats hands-on training. Attend a workshop at a local irrigation training centre â many are subsidized.

Beware of fake products. Buy from established shops, not roadside vendors. Check for brand names like Netafim, Rivulis, or Jain. If a deal seems too good, it probably is. Build relationships: pay on time, be clear about your needs, and ask for discounts on bulk orders. A good supplier will become a long-term partner, helping you troubleshoot and expand.

lessons.title: Evaluating and Improving Your System Over Time
lessons.body:
After one season, evaluate your system. Did it deliver enough water? Did crops suffer? Check your records: how many hours did you run the pump? How much did you harvest? Compare with your water audit targets. For example, if you planned 25,000 litres per day but only applied 20,000, your yields may be lower. Measure soil moisture: dig a hole 15 cm deep and squeeze the soil. If it crumbles, it's too dry; if it forms a ball, it's good. Do this weekly.

Look for signs of inefficiency. Are there dry spots? They may be due to clogged emitters or uneven pressure. Flush the lines and check the filter. If pressure is low at the end of the line, your mainline is too small or the pump is weak. Measure flow at the last emitter: it should be within 10% of the first. If not, install a pressure regulator or divide the field into smaller blocks.

Track costs and benefits. Add up all expenses (pump, pipes, labour, repairs) and compare to extra income from higher yields. If you spent $500 and earned $800 more, your profit is $300. Calculate payback period: total cost Ã· annual extra profit. If it's more than 3 years, look for cheaper improvements. For example, adding mulch can reduce water use by 30%, saving pumping costs.

Improve by upgrading: add a timer to automate irrigation, install a fertigation unit to inject fertilizer, or switch to solar power to cut fuel costs. Learn from other farmers â visit their farms and ask what works. Keep a simple logbook: date, crop, irrigation hours, problems, and fixes. After 2-3 seasons, you will know exactly what your system can do. Then you can expand or refine. Remember, irrigation is not a one-time project â it's a continuous cycle of monitoring, learning, and improving.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Planning and Implementing Your Irrigation Project

This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in this module into a working toolkit for smallholder farmers, cooperatives, and agripreneurs across Africa. Irrigation is not a piece of equipment â it is a business decision. Every pump, pipe, and emitter you install must pay for itself through higher yields, better timing, or reduced risk. This reference gives you the numbers, tables, and checklists to make that happen, whether you farm 0.5 hectares in Kenya or 5 hectares in Ghana.

1. The Farm Water Audit: Know Your Supply Before You Buy

A water audit answers three questions: How much water do you have? How much do your crops need? What is the gap? Start with your source â borehole, river, dam, or rainwater tank. Measure, don't guess. A simple bucket-and-stopwatch test gives you flow rate in litres per minute. Multiply by the hours you can realistically pump per day to get daily volume. Then compare this with crop water requirements, which in most of sub-Saharan Africa range from 4â8 mm/day depending on crop and season. One millimetre over one hectare equals 10,000 litres. So a 1-hectare maize field needing 6 mm/day requires 60,000 litres daily â that is 60 mÂ³. If your borehole yields 30 litres per minute and you can pump 8 hours, you have 14,400 litres â a serious shortfall. Knowing this before you buy saves you from buying the wrong pump.

2. Designing a Custom Irrigation Plan

There is no universal irrigation design. Your plan must match your soil, slope, crop, labour, and budget. The table below summarises the four main system types relevant to African smallholders.

Table 1: Irrigation System Selection Guide for African Smallholders
System Efficiency Best For Capital Cost (USD/ha) Labour Need Key Limitation
Surface / Furrow 40â60% Rice, sugarcane, fodder 200â800 High Waterlogging, erosion
Sprinkler 70â80% Vegetables, maize, wheat 1,500â3,500 Medium Wind losses, high pressure
Drip 85â95% Tomatoes, peppers, orchards 2,000â5,000 Low Clogging, initial cost
Manual / Bucket 30â50% Seedlings, small plots 50â200 Very high Back-breaking, slow

Sources: FAO AQUASTAT country data; ICARDA/IFAD smallholder irrigation cost studies (2019â2023); Africa Rice Center (AfricaRice) technical bulletins.

Your design must also account for soil type. Sandy soils hold little water and need frequent, small applications â ideal for drip. Clay soils hold more but drain slowly â better for furrow or sprinkler with careful scheduling. A simple infiltration test (dig a 30 cm hole, fill with water, time how long it takes to drain) tells you which approach fits. For most African smallholders, the sweet spot is a hybrid: drip for high-value crops near the homestead, and sprinkler or furrow for staple crops in larger fields.

3. Cost Estimation and Funding Options

Irrigation projects fail when costs are underestimated. The table below breaks down typical costs for a 1-hectare drip system in East Africa. Use it as a template, but get local quotes â prices vary by 30â50% between countries and seasons.

Table 2: Indicative Cost Breakdown for 1 ha Drip Irrigation (East Africa, 2024)
Item Specification Cost (USD) % of Total
Water source development Borehole or dam upgrade 800â2,500 25â35%
Pump & power Solar or diesel, 1â2 HP 400â1,200 15â20%
Mainline & sub-main pipes PVC or HDPE, 50â63 mm 300â700 10â15%
Drip lines & emitters 16 mm laterals, 30 cm spacing 600â1,200 20â25%
Filtration & valves Sand filter, screen, ball valves 200â500 7â10%
Installation labour Local technician + helpers 150â400 5â8%
Contingency (10%) â 250â600 10%
Total â 2,700â7,100 100%

Sources: SNV Netherlands Development Organisation irrigation cost surveys (Kenya, Tanzania, Ethiopia); FAO Investment Centre reports; KALRO technical notes.

Funding options in Africa include: (1) Savings and group contributions â SACCOs and village savings groups are the most common first source; (2) Microfinance â institutions like Kiva, Tala, and national MFIs offer 6â24 month loans at 15â30% APR; (3) Government subsidies â Kenya's National Irrigation Authority, Ghana's MiDA, and Ethiopia's Small-Scale Irrigation Program offer cost-share grants; (4) Development partners â IFAD, GIZ, and USAID Feed the Future programs; (5) Equipment leasing â some suppliers now offer pay-as-you-irrigate models. Always calculate your payback period: if the system costs $4,000 and adds $1,500/year in net income, payback is under 3 years â viable. If it takes 10 years, reconsider.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Water Safety and Electrical Hazards

Never install a pump or electrical panel near standing water without proper earthing and RCD (residual current device) protection. In many African rural settings, electrical codes are poorly enforced â this kills. Use solar pumps where possible to eliminate electrocution risk. Never enter a dam, well, or pit without a second person present and a safety line. Test water quality (especially borehole water) for salinity and heavy metals before using it on vegetables â contaminated water enters the food chain directly. Store fuel for diesel pumps away from the pump house and never refuel a hot engine.

4. Phased Implementation for Small Budgets

You do not need $5,000 on day one. Phase your investment:

  • Phase 1 (Month 0â3): Water audit, soil test, and a 0.25 ha trial plot using manual or low-cost drip. Cost: $200â500.
  • Phase 2 (Month 4â9): Add a solar pump and expand to 0.5 ha. Reinvest first harvest income. Cost: $800â1,500.
  • Phase 3 (Month 10â18): Scale to 1 ha, add filtration, and install a small storage tank (5,000â10,000 L) to buffer supply. Cost: $1,500â3,000.
  • Phase 4 (Year 2+): Optimise with soil moisture sensors, fertigation, and a second crop cycle. Cost: $500â1,500.

This approach reduces risk, builds skills incrementally, and lets you learn from real results before committing larger sums. It also makes you more attractive to lenders â they see a track record, not just a plan.

5. Working with Local Suppliers and Experts

Your success depends on who you buy from and who installs your system. In Africa, the irrigation supply chain is fragmented. Follow these rules:

  • Visit the supplier's yard. See the pipes, pumps, and emitters physically. Ask for references from other farmers in your area.
  • Insist on a written quotation with brand names, specifications, and warranty terms. Verbal deals collapse when things break.
  • Check for local spare parts. A pump that needs a part from China will sit idle for months. Buy brands with regional distributors â Grundfos, Pedrollo, and Dayliff have strong African presence.
  • Hire a certified installer or train a local technician. A poorly installed drip system leaks 30% of water and fails within a year.
  • Join a farmer cooperative â group purchasing reduces costs by 15â30% and gives you bargaining power for maintenance services.

6. Evaluating and Improving Your System Over Time

An irrigation system is not "install and forget." Monitor these indicators monthly:

  • Application uniformity: Place cups at different points along a drip line. If some get 50 ml and others get 200 ml, your system is unbalanced â clean filters and check pressure.
  • Energy cost per mÂ³: Track fuel or electricity used per cubic metre pumped. If it rises, your pump is wearing out or your pipes are leaking.
  • Crop yield per mÂ³: This is your ultimate business metric. If you are not improving it, your irrigation is not paying.
  • Maintenance log: Record every filter clean, emitter replacement, and pump service. This data helps you predict failures and budget for replacements.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. â Measure your water source flow rate (litres/minute) and daily availability before designing anything.
  2. â Calculate crop water demand in mm/day and convert to litres for your field size.
  3. â Test soil infiltration rate and texture to select the right irrigation method.
  4. â Get at least three written quotes with brand names and warranty terms.
  5. â Calculate payback period â if over 5 years, redesign or phase the project.
  6. â Install a storage tank (minimum 1 day of demand) to buffer supply and reduce pump cycling.
  7. â Train at least one person on your farm to clean filters, flush lines, and spot leaks weekly.
  8. â Keep a simple logbook of water used, energy cost, and yield per plot â review monthly.

Further Reading

  • FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56: Crop Evapotranspiration â the global standard for calculating crop water needs.
  • FAO AQUASTAT â country-level water resources and irrigation data for all African nations.
  • IFAD Smallholder Irrigation Market Initiative â practical guides on market-led irrigation for African smallholders.
  • International Water Management Institute (IWMI) â research on sustainable irrigation in Africa and Asia.
  • Africa Rice Center (AfricaRice) â technical bulletins on water management for rice and diversified crops.

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills programme. All costs and figures are indicative and should be validated with local suppliers and extension officers before investment.

quiz.q: What is the first step in conducting a farm water audit?
quiz.explanation: Measuring water sources gives you the supply baseline before calculating demand.

quiz.q: If a 20-litre bucket fills in 10 seconds, what is the flow rate in litres per minute?
quiz.explanation: 20 litres in 10 seconds = 2 litres per second Ã 60 = 120 litres per minute.

quiz.q: How many litres are in 1 mm of water over 1 hectare?
quiz.explanation: 1 mm over 1 ha = 1 litre per mÂ² Ã 10,000 mÂ² = 10,000 litres.

quiz.q: For a 0.5 ha plot of tomatoes needing 5 mm/day, what is the daily water requirement?
quiz.explanation: 0.5 ha Ã 5 mm Ã 10,000 litres/ha/mm = 25,000 litres.

quiz.q: What is a typical pH range for most crops?
quiz.explanation: Most crops grow best at pH 6.0-7.0 for nutrient availability.

quiz.q: Which irrigation method saves 30-50% water compared to furrow?
quiz.explanation: Drip delivers water directly to roots, reducing evaporation and runoff.

quiz.q: If you have 33,333 emitters each giving 1 litre/hour, how long to deliver 50,000 litres?
quiz.explanation: 50,000 Ã· 1 = 50,000 emitter-hours Ã· 33,333 = 1.5 hours.

quiz.q: What is the precipitation rate of a sprinkler delivering 30 litres/min over 113 mÂ²?
quiz.explanation: 30 litres/min Ã· 113 mÂ² = 0.265 mm/min (since 1 litre/mÂ² = 1 mm).

quiz.q: What size pump is needed for 104 litres/min at 15 m head with 60% efficiency?
Which component prevents clogging in a drip system?
quiz.explanation: Filters remove particles that would block emitters.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of drip lines for 0.5 ha at $0.20/m?
Which funding option typically has the lowest interest rate?
quiz.explanation: Personal savings have no interest, though opportunity cost exists.

quiz.q: What is a good way to reduce irrigation costs?
quiz.explanation: Phasing spreads costs and reduces risk while generating income.

quiz.q: In phased implementation, what is a reasonable first phase size?
quiz.explanation: Starting with 0.1 ha keeps initial costs low and manageable.

quiz.q: What percentage of profits should be reinvested in expansion?
quiz.explanation: Reinvesting at least 30% allows steady growth without debt.

quiz.q: What does mulch do for irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Mulch covers soil, reducing evaporation and conserving water.

quiz.q: Who can provide free advice on irrigation in your area?
quiz.explanation: Extension officers are trained and usually free.

quiz.q: What should you check before buying a pump?
quiz.explanation: Flow rate and head must match your water audit needs.

quiz.q: What wall thickness of drip tape lasts 3-5 seasons?
quiz.explanation: Thicker walls (0.4 mm) resist damage and last longer.

quiz.q: How often should you clean a drip filter?
quiz.explanation: Weekly cleaning prevents clogging and maintains flow.

quiz.q: What is a sign of clogged emitters?
quiz.explanation: Dry spots indicate emitters are blocked and not delivering water.

quiz.q: How can you check soil moisture simply?
quiz.explanation: Squeezing soil shows if it's too dry or moist.

quiz.q: If flow at the last emitter is 20% less than the first, what should you do?
quiz.explanation: Pressure regulator evens out flow across the system.

quiz.q: What is payback period?
options: B) Total cost Ã· annual extra profit
quiz.explanation: Payback period shows how long to recover investment.

quiz.q: What upgrade can automate irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Timers turn pumps on and off automatically.

quiz.q: Why keep a logbook?
options: B) To track problems and fixes
quiz.explanation: Logbook helps identify patterns and improve decisions.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of solar pumps?
quiz.explanation: Solar pumps have no fuel costs after installation.

quiz.q: What does EC measure in water?
quiz.explanation: EC (electrical conductivity) indicates salt content.

quiz.q: Which crop is salt-tolerant?
quiz.explanation: Spinach can tolerate higher salinity than many crops.

quiz.q: What is the recommended emitter spacing for vegetables?
quiz.explanation: 0.3 m spacing is common for close-planted vegetables.
